lectures.name: Understanding and Managing Chronic Pain
lectures.title: Understanding and managing chronic pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Chronic pain is mostly sensitized (neuropathic) pain that outlasts the injury, so "hurt is not harm" and the treatment with excellent evidence is exercise, not passive therapy. Massage is the only passive modality that works, and only with exercise and education. SSRIs do little for pain; tricyclics and SNRIs (norepinephrine) do. Gabapentinoids are for neuropathic pain; their main side effect is sedation. NSAIDs: a 2-3 week trial. Watchful opioid dose 90 mg morphine equivalent per day; strong recommendation against opioids after addiction.

Most chronic pain is no longer a tissue problem but a processing problem: the nervous system has been turned up (central sensitization), so the plan aims at function, not cure - education, activity and a multimodal drug plan, with opioids last and only under the START rules.
1. How pain normally travels and is turned up or down

• Fibres: A-beta = touch, vibration · A-delta = heat, cold, sharp pain · C = chemical pain · they release glutamate in the dorsal horn, where NMDA receptors are normally blocked by magnesium
  • Spinothalamic tract → thalamus → medial system (cingulate, insula, amygdala: the emotional "suffering") and lateral system (somatosensory cortex: where it hurts)
  • Central sensitization ("wind-up"): repeated input removes the magnesium block → the second-order neuron becomes hyperexcitable → the same stimulus gives a bigger signal
  • Three ways pain is dampened
    • gate control: A-beta input switches on inhibitory interneurons, so rubbing a sore spot helps
    • endogenous opioids (enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins) hyperpolarize the neurons before and after the synapse
    • descending inhibition from the brainstem uses norepinephrine and serotonin - more of both = more pain inhibition

blocks.cap: Gate control: A-beta touch fibres switch on the inhibitory interneuron; C fibres switch it off

blocks.html: 2. Types of pain and how long it lasts

rows: Seconds, at the same time as the cause
Can outlast tissue healing · a disease in itself · big emotional component

blocks.html:
• Neuropathic pain = from a lesion (inflammation) or dysfunction (ectopic firing) of the nervous system itself
    • described as burning, electric, shooting, pins and needles, numbness
    • peripheral: diabetic and other length-dependent neuropathy · radiculopathy · post-herpetic neuralgia · trigeminal neuralgia · central: thalamus, brainstem or cord lesions · phantom limb

blocks.cap: Neuropathic vs nociceptive pain: how each is described and behaves

blocks.html: 3. Chronic pain: two kinds, and what it does to the person

• Chronic nociceptive (the minority): nociceptors keep firing, e.g. chronic inflammatory disease, osteoarthritis · easy to localize · treat by stopping the ongoing activation
  • Chronic neuropathic (the majority): the injury has healed but processing is abnormal
    • wind-up · more glutamate (NMDA) receptors · less descending serotonin and norepinephrine · pain-avoidant behaviour
  • Mood: a shared serotonin and norepinephrine imbalance links pain and depression
    • comorbid depression is common (sources differ: the note says up to ~90%, the upper-year notes over 50% - check the slides)
    • predictors of depression: pain intensity · number of painful areas · frequency of severe pain · other psychosocial factors
    • anxiety → activity avoidance → deconditioning, social isolation
  • Learned avoidance: moving hurts → stop moving, which spreads to anything that might hurt (operant conditioning) · pain tied to a setting such as work (classical conditioning)
4. The approach to chronic pain

blocks.html: 5. The team

• The family physician coordinates most care · refer to a multidisciplinary chronic pain clinic when: not responding to standard analgesics · management needs review · activity, mood and social life are deteriorating
  • Clinic roles: physicians (anesthesia, neurology, rehabilitation, internal medicine, psychiatry) review, trial drugs, give interventions, hand a long-term plan back · nurses support and triage · psychologists: therapy for depression and anxiety, cognitive behavioural therapy, education · occupational and physiotherapists: pacing, return to activity
6. Non-drug management

• Education - "hurt does not equal harm": the injury has usually healed; the pain comes from faulty signal processing · returning to activity desensitizes the system · exercise releases endorphins
  • Exercise and activity - excellent evidence
    • strengthening + flexibility + cardiovascular work · spinal pain: core strength and flexibility · yoga and tai chi beat general exercise for back pain
    • works best when individualized, supervised, stretching and strengthening · any regular activity matters more than the exact exercise
    • work hardening programs are not effective
  • Passive modalities (laser, ultrasound, heat, acupuncture, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation): very little evidence, used because patients ask · they reinforce the idea that tissue damage causes the pain
    • nerve stimulation: slightly better than placebo, an add-on only · massage is the only one that works, and only with exercise and education
    • spinal manipulation: a short course under 6 weeks may help, no evidence after 6 weeks
7. Drugs for chronic pain

rows: Block cyclooxygenase (blocking COX-1 causes the harm)
Gastrointestinal bleeding and ulcer (less with COX-2) · kidney injury · raised blood pressure · 2-3 week trial, then monitor
Max 4 g/day (2 g in liver disease)
Less prostaglandin in the central nervous system
Alone, or with an opioid to lower its dose
amitriptyline, nortriptyline - 10-50 mg for pain and sleep
gabapentin 900-2700 mg/day · pregabalin 75-300 mg twice daily
Block the alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit → less glutamate and substance P released
nabilone · cannabis with a high cannabidiol to tetrahydrocannabinol ratio

blocks.html: • Multimodal at the lowest effective doses · match the drug to the coexisting problem, then trial and error, one at a time (switch for side effects, or no effect after a month at the top dose) · topical capsaicin or lidocaine for neuropathic pain
8. Opioids: the START principle

• S - Should I start? Pain, medical, psychosocial, psychiatric and substance use history (personal and family)
    • Opioid Risk Tool: highest risk = male · age 16-45 · personal or family substance use · psychiatric history · urine drug screen at baseline and at random
    • evidence: medium effect on pain, small on function · only tramadol helps fibromyalgia · not for migraine, tension headache or irritable bowel syndrome
    • taper off benzodiazepines (sedation, overdose) · informed consent · signed treatment agreement
  • T - Trial: no driving until the dose is stable · start low, go slow · aim for better function or at least 30% less pain, stop rising when benefit plateaus or side effects appear · watchful dose: 90 mg morphine equivalent per day
  • A - Monitor: analgesia · daily activities · adverse effects (nausea, constipation, drowsiness, low sex hormones, worse sleep apnea, opioid-induced hyperalgesia) · aberrant behaviour (early refills, crushing or injecting, double-doctoring)
  • R - Restrict: history of addiction - strong recommendation against (if used, under 20 mg morphine equivalent per day) · active psychiatric disorder - weak recommendation against, stabilize first · elderly - lower, slower, longer intervals, stop benzodiazepines · adolescents - only after other drugs fail · pregnancy - taper to lowest dose or off
  • T - Terminate for addiction, misuse or poor effect
    • switching opioids: from a high dose give 50% or less of the morphine equivalent, from a moderate or low dose 60-70%
    • tapering: 10% of the daily dose per day up to per month · slow by half once a third is left · watch for withdrawal (nausea, diarrhea, aches, chills, pain flare, anxiety, anger)

blocks.cap: Stepped approach: non-opioid analgesics and adjuvants, then weak opioids, then strong opioids

lectures.name: Psychological Factors in Managing Chronic Pain
lectures.title: Psychological factors in managing chronic pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Up to half of chronic pain patients have comorbid major depression, and it predicts that the pain will persist - so distress that impairs function needs its own diagnosis. Factitious disorder: no external reward (gain unconscious); malingering: an external reward (conscious). Conversion disorder is diagnosed only after everything else is excluded. Pacing = less on good days, more on bad days. CBT for pain targets mental filter, catastrophizing and emotional reasoning; avoid progressive muscle relaxation.

Pain and mood feed each other: the lecture asks you to spot when distress has become its own diagnosis (a mood, anxiety or substance disorder, or a somatic symptom and related disorder), and then to manage chronic pain psychologically as well as physically - managed, not cured.
1. How big the problem is

• About 20% of Canadians live with chronic non-cancer pain · half have had it over 10 years
  • Higher in marginalized groups and people living in poverty
2. Assessing chronic pain

• History and exam
    • duration and nature of the pain
    • associated symptoms, physical and psychological - including suicidal thoughts
    • past care: treatments, alternative therapies, medications, home remedies - what worked and what did not
    • effect on function
  • Charting the pain: descriptive words · 0-10 numeric score · face scales (children) · visual analogue scale · multidimensional tools (McGill Pain Questionnaire)
  • Pain diary: the situation, the sensation, physical and psychological distress rated separately, what was done - shows the patient that pain and distress do not always move together

blocks.cap: Pain scales: verbal, visual analogue, 0-10 numeric and faces

blocks.html: 3. Pain is shaped by the mind

• Pain is subjective but multidimensional, shaped bottom-up and top-down by: past pain · attention to pain · expectations · mood (depression, anxiety) · sensitization
  • Objective markers that track it: pain behaviours · physiological measures · change in function
  • Fear-avoidance cycle: avoid what hurts → disuse, disability, low mood → more pain → more fear
    • catastrophizing feeds the cycle · broken by confronting the pain and accepting it is not harmful

blocks.cap: Fear-avoidance model: catastrophizing and fear lead to avoidance and disability; confrontation leads to recovery

blocks.html: 4. When distress is more than chronic pain
Significant or prolonged distress that impairs function → consider another diagnosis, alongside or instead of chronic pain.

blocks.html: Comorbid mental disorders

• Major depression in up to 50% - a significant predictor that pain will persist
    • linked to more disability, negative thoughts about pain, pain intensity and life interference · less sense of control · more passive-avoidant coping
  • Anxiety: symptoms in 50% · an anxiety disorder (panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder) in 20-30% · after a trauma or accident think post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or acute stress disorder
  • Substance use disorders are more common, including opioid use disorder after injury
Medically unexplained symptoms = persistent bodily complaints with no structural or pathological cause found

• seen in over 60% of neurology referrals · three kinds: pain in different places · disturbed organ function · fatigue
  • functional somatic syndromes: irritable bowel syndrome, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia · more often female · overlap with depression and anxiety
  • the DSM-5 regrouped these as somatic symptom and related disorders, moving away from mind-body dualism and the idea that the symptoms are "not real"

rows: Emotional or behavioural symptoms within 3 months of an identifiable stressor
Chronic distress and worry about one or more bodily symptoms
Altered voluntary motor or sensory function (weakness, paralysis, seizures, blindness) with no neurological or medical cause found
Presents self or another (by proxy) as ill or injured; may make themselves sick
Distress out of proportion to the stressor and/or impaired functioning
Prevalence 5-7% · repeated visits to family doctors, walk-ins, emergency
Acute (under 6 months) or persistent · with or without a psychological stressor
Unnecessary tests and treatment - diagnose it so it can be managed psychologically
Diagnose only after ruling out everything else - some later prove to have a disease that explains it

blocks.html: 5. Psychosocial management

• Multimodal and multidisciplinary, almost always · "start with the patient": realistic, measurable goals · set the expectation that pain can be well managed, not necessarily cured
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT): links thoughts, feelings and behaviours to pain · aims to manage, not cure · few randomized trials, but they are mostly positive
    • targets cognitive distortions: mental filter (noticing only the negatives) · catastrophizing (expecting the worst) · emotional reasoning (it feels true, so it must be)
    • other parts: patient and family education · contingency management (antecedent → behaviour → consequence that reinforces it) · relaxation training (avoid progressive muscle relaxation) · problem-solving · communication · distraction · behavioural activation · cognitive restructuring
    • groups help: a peer with chronic pain can connect better than a clinician
  • Psychodynamic (insight-oriented) therapy: a secondary option for lifelong behaviour patterns
  • Relaxation and meditation: pain → sympathetic surge → clenched muscles, higher blood pressure and heart rate → more pain · deep breathing switches on the parasympathetic side · refocusing on the breath
  • Rehabilitation
    • ergonomics, "new ways to do old things"
    • pacing: limit activity on good days and push a little on flare days, instead of overdoing it then spending days in bed
    • exercise · vocational counselling and work modifications to return to work

blocks.cap: The cognitive behavioural cycle: thoughts create feelings, feelings create behaviour, behaviour reinforces thoughts

blocks.html: 6. Secondary prevention and general tips

• Prevent loss of function, and start before lifestyle is disrupted (the upper-year notes put this at about 12 weeks)
  • Focus on health, behaviour and what the patient can do, not on "medical problems" · the patient must be an active participant
  • Talk to the workplace, family and caregivers · keep reassessing and adjusting
  • Tips: one physician, regular visits · goal-directed · notice direct and indirect communication · limit investigations and operations (but chronic pain patients still get acute problems) · motivational interviewing · watch your own biases

lectures.name: Introduction to Neurology
lectures.title: Introduction to neurology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Localize first: upper motor neuron = high tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski positive; lower motor neuron = low tone, reduced reflexes, Babinski negative. -plegia is paralysis, -paresis is weakness. Dysarthria is articulation; aphasia is language. Middle cerebral artery stroke: face and arm worse than leg. Weak eyes and swallowing point to the neuromuscular junction; generalized proximal weakness to muscle.

Neurology is a method before it is a list of diseases: describe the problem in the right words, localize the lesion, then build the differential and the plan. The first fork is always central (upper motor neuron) or peripheral (lower motor neuron).
1. Why it matters

• About 10% of family practice visits are for a neurological symptom
  • Neurology turns up across specialties: seizures on the ward, strokes as a cardiovascular complication
2. The vocabulary

rows: Paraplegia (both legs) · hemiplegia (one side) · quadriplegia (all four limbs)
Cerebellar (motor coordination) · vestibular (balance) · sensory (sense of position)

blocks.html:
• Level of consciousness, from normal down: conscious → disoriented (confused, slow, cannot follow instructions) → delirium (restless, agitated, poor attention) → somnolent (drowsy) → obtunded (reduced alertness, slow to react) → coma (no response, no corneal or gag reflex, pupils do not react to light)
  • Dominant hemisphere = where language lives · left in right-handed people · left-handed people: left, right or both
  • Middle cerebral artery = main supply of the lateral brain · a stroke gives contralateral face and arm weaker than leg, because of where they sit on the homunculus

blocks.alt: motor and sensory homunculus - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Motor (precentral) and sensory (postcentral) homunculus: face and hand lateral, leg medial

blocks.html: 3. The clinical approach

• Four steps: describe the problem → localize the lesion → differential diagnosis → plan
  • First question: central or peripheral?

cols: Upper motor neuron (brain and spinal cord)
Lower motor neuron (anterior horn cell out to the muscle)

blocks.html: • The spinal cord ends at L1; below that are nerve roots (cauda equina), so lesions there are lower motor neuron

or lumbar roots"] B -->|"Lower: low tone, reduced reflexes"| G{"Pattern?"} G -->|"One myotome"| H["NERVE ROOT"] G -->|"One limb, several nerves"| I["PLEXUS"] G -->|"One nerve, or several separate nerves"| J["PERIPHERAL NERVE(S)"] G -->|"Eyes and swallowing"| K["NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION"] G -->|"Generalized, proximal"| L["MUSCLE"]

blocks.html: 4. How the nervous system is built

• Myelin
    • peripheral nerves: each Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon; segments are separated by nodes of Ranvier, which make conduction fast · a Schwann cell can also ensheath many unmyelinated axons
    • central nervous system: one oligodendrocyte myelinates many segments
  • Spinal cord: cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral segments · white matter outside, grey inside · sensory tracts ascend, motor tracts descend
  • Planes: coronal · axial · sagittal

blocks.cap: Coronal, axial and sagittal planes of the brain

lectures.name: Introduction to Neuroanatomy
lectures.title: Introduction to neuroanatomy
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Brainstem nuclei go 2-4-4: midbrain III-IV, pons V-VIII, medulla IX-XII (I and II come off the forebrain). CT for a quick look for blood; FLAIR MRI for white matter. Basal ganglia and cerebellum damage give movement problems without weakness. Spinothalamic = pain and temperature; dorsal columns = vibration and position. Middle meningeal artery rupture → epidural hematoma.

A map to hang the rest of neuro on: where things are (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain; the lobes; the brainstem and its cranial nerve nuclei; the tracts, ventricles and vessels) and what each one does - so that a symptom can be traced back to a place.
1. Basic organization

• Grey matter = neuron cell bodies · white matter = myelinated axon tracts
  • Central nervous system = brain + spinal cord · peripheral nervous system = spinal and cranial nerves, ganglia, sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves
  • Function: sensory afferents (toward the central nervous system) → integration → motor efferents (away from it)
2. Orientation and imaging

• Rostral-caudal and dorsal-ventral switch direction between brain and spinal cord, because the developing neural tube bends
  • Planes: coronal (front-to-back slices) · axial (parallel to the horizon) · sagittal (left-right slices)

rows: Telling brain tissue from fluid and other tissue
No cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal → white matter abnormalities stand out

blocks.html: 3. Divisions of the brain

rows: Telencephalon: cerebral cortex + deep structures (basal ganglia) · diencephalon: thalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus
Cerebral peduncles · superior and inferior colliculi

blocks.alt: embryologic divisions of the brain (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain).jpg
blocks.cap: Forebrain (telencephalon, diencephalon), midbrain and hindbrain on a sagittal brain

blocks.html: 4. Cerebral cortex and lobes

• Gyri = ridges · sulci = shallow grooves · fissures = deep grooves that divide lobes · the brain is smooth until about 6 months, then folds to fit the skull
  • Central sulcus: frontal from parietal · lateral sulcus: temporal from the rest

rows: Voluntary movement (primary motor cortex, precentral gyrus) · planning movement (premotor) · eye movements (frontal eye field) · speech production (Broca's area) · executive function (prefrontal)

Sensation (primary somatosensory cortex, postcentral gyrus) · spatial awareness · understanding speech (Wernicke's area - sources differ: the note puts it in the parietal lobe, the upper-year notes in the posterior temporal lobe - check the slides)
Hearing (primary auditory cortex) · smell · recognizing faces, words, objects (fusiform gyrus) · memory

blocks.html: 5. Deep structures

• Basal ganglia: deep forebrain nuclei that turn cortical activity into one motor output - select the wanted movement and suppress the others
    • damage: no weakness, but trouble starting movement, stiffness, slowness (parkinsonism) or extra movements · contributes to Tourette syndrome
  • Cerebellum: smooth, fine coordination - damage gives incoordination without weakness
  • Thalamus (diencephalon): the relay for sensory and motor information · links to the limbic system (memory, emotion), basal ganglia (movement) and primary sensory cortices
6. Brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei

rows: Superior, middle and inferior peduncles (the cerebellum grows out of the pons)

blocks.html:
• CN I and II come straight off the forebrain, not the brainstem
  • Medulla = vital autonomic control (breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, digestion)

blocks.cap: Cranial nerve nuclei by level: midbrain 2, pons 4, medulla 4

blocks.html: 7. Spinal cord tracts

rows: Fine touch, vibration, position · gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm
Pain, temperature and touch to the thalamus
Motor cortex → brainstem (muscles of facial expression)

blocks.html: 8. Ventricles and vessels

• Ventricles: two C-shaped lateral (anterior, posterior, inferior horns) → third (between the thalami) → cerebral aqueduct → fourth (between cerebellum and brainstem) · CSF is made by the choroid plexus
  • Blood-brain barrier = tight junctions + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes + pericytes · lipid-soluble drugs diffuse across; polar ones need active transport
  • Middle meningeal artery (external carotid branch) supplies the dura · rupture → epidural hematoma
  • Circle of Willis: anterior cerebral · anterior communicating · internal carotid · posterior communicating · posterior cerebral (sources differ: the note includes the middle cerebral artery; the upper-year notes and the cranial cavity note say it is not part of the circle - check the slides)
  • Dural venous sinuses (superior and inferior sagittal, straight, transverse, sigmoid) take cerebral veins and CSF (via arachnoid granulations) → internal jugular vein

lectures.name: Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function
lectures.title: Cranial nerve anatomy and function
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Forehead spared = upper motor neuron (central) facial palsy; forehead involved and eye will not close = lower motor neuron (Bell's palsy). Double vision is never from a lesion above the brainstem. Third nerve compression: think posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Corneal reflex = V1 in, VII out; gag = IX in, X out. Tongue deviates toward the lesion; wasting and fasciculations say lower motor neuron. Do not test smell with a noxious stimulus.

Twelve nerves, one question each time: what does this nerve carry, how do I test it, and what does a lesion look like? The cranial nerves and their nuclei are peripheral, so a nerve lesion gives lower motor neuron signs; the trick is telling it from an upper motor neuron (cortical or brainstem) cause.
1. The ground rules

• Cranial nerves = 12 pairs of nerve bundles that leave the cranial cavity · their nuclei and nerves belong to the peripheral nervous system
  • Fibres are sensory, motor, parasympathetic, or a mix
  • No sympathetic fibres start in a cranial nerve: sympathetics leave the thoracolumbar cord, climb the sympathetic trunk, synapse in the cervical ganglia, then hitch a ride on other nerves to the head

blocks.cap: The 12 cranial nerves leaving the base of the brain, with their targets

blocks.html: 2. The twelve nerves

Reduced smell · trauma · Kallmann syndrome · inferior frontal lobe tumour · after a virus (COVID-19)

Reduced vision, trouble focusing · optic neuritis · ischemic optic neuropathy · tumour compression

Most eye muscles (sources differ: the note lists superior, inferior and medial rectus; the upper-year notes add levator palpebrae and a fourth extraocular muscle - check the slides) · pupil constriction · lens accommodation
Eye movements · pupillary light reflex · look for ptosis

Facial sensation: V1 forehead and cornea (also carries sympathetics to the pupil dilator) · V2 mid face · V3 lower face + muscles of chewing
Light touch in each division · corneal reflex (sensory limb, V1) · clench the jaw (V3)
Numb face or one division ± neuropathic pain · nerve: compression, inflammation, trigeminal neuralgia · central: brainstem stroke or multiple sclerosis, thalamus or cortex

Hearing loss, vertigo · inner ear · the nerve (vestibular neuritis) · brainstem stroke

Gag reflex (sensory limb) · say "ah" (uvula pulled to the normal side)
Trouble swallowing, slurred speech, dry mouth, less taste
Palate and larynx (the recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch) · sensation of pharynx and larynx · slows heart, gut
Say "ah": palate rises evenly · gag (motor limb) · voice

XI Accessory (up through foramen magnum, out the jugular foramen)
Turn the head each way · shrug
Wasting of both muscles · rarely tested

blocks.html: 3. Facial weakness: upper or lower motor neuron?

rows: Cannot close; the eye may roll up on trying
Bell's palsy (sudden, with taste loss) · parotid tumour

blocks.cap: Central facial palsy spares the forehead; peripheral facial palsy does not

blocks.html: 4. Patterns across the nerves

• III, IV, VI - double vision: always means a brainstem, cranial nerve, eye muscle or neuromuscular junction problem - never a lesion above the brainstem · test the "H", the pupils and the eyelid
  • V - numbness: whole face vs one division tells you whether the lesion is before or after the trigeminal nucleus
  • IX and X - bulbar symptoms (slurred speech, hoarseness, trouble swallowing): lower motor neuron = brainstem or skull base · upper motor neuron = cortical or subcortical control of speech and swallowing
  • XII: the tongue deviates to the weak side in both upper and lower motor neuron lesions · wasting and fasciculations mean lower motor neuron

lectures.name: Facial Anatomy
lectures.title: Facial anatomy
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The facial nerve (VII) moves the face; the trigeminal nerve (V) feels it, and V3 also works the chewing muscles. The angle of the jaw is not trigeminal - it is the great auricular nerve (C2-C3). Supraorbital, infraorbital and mental foramina = V1, V2, V3. Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; frontalis raises the brow. The facial nerve branches inside the parotid gland. Masseter protrudes the jaw; temporalis retracts it.

The face has two nerves that are easy to mix up: the facial nerve (CN VII) moves the face, the trigeminal nerve (CN V) feels it and chews. Learn the structures by layer - bone and foramina, muscles, vessels, nerves - and each finding traces back to one of them.
1. Bones and foramina

• Facial skeleton (viscerocranium): jaw, nose and part of the orbit
    • nasal bones · maxilla · zygomatic bone · mandible · the frontal bone forms the forehead
  • Foramina carry the trigeminal sensory branches out to the skin:
2. Muscles
• Muscles of facial expression start as one sheet over face, scalp and neck, then form sphincters and dilators of the eyes, nose and mouth · they insert into the skin · all supplied by CN VII

rows: Blows out the cheeks · keeps food between the teeth when chewing

blocks.html:
• Muscles of chewing act on the temporomandibular joint · supplied by CN V3
    • masseter: closes the jaw strongly, protrudes it · temporalis: closes the jaw strongly, retracts it

blocks.cap: Muscles of facial expression: frontalis, orbicularis oculi and oris, zygomaticus major, buccinator, occipitalis, platysma

blocks.html: 3. Parotid gland

• One of the three paired salivary glands · superficial to the masseter, in front of the ear · wrapped in the investing fascia of the neck
  • Its duct crosses the masseter, then pierces the buccinator to open into the mouth
  • The facial nerve runs through it and splits into its five branches there
4. Vessels

• Arteries come mainly from the external carotid artery
    • Facial artery: runs diagonally from near the angle of the mandible to the inner corner of the eye
    • superficial temporal artery: the end of the external carotid, up the side of the scalp
  • Veins vary a lot between people
    • maxillary vein (from the pterygoid plexus) + superficial temporal vein → retromandibular vein, in the parotid
    • posterior division + posterior auricular vein → external jugular vein
    • anterior division + facial vein → common facial vein → internal jugular vein
5. Nerves
• Facial nerve (CN VII) - motor: enters the parotid and divides into five branches, top to bottom: temporal · zygomatic · buccal · marginal mandibular · cervical (see the muscle table)

blocks.cap: The five branches of the facial nerve fanning out from the parotid gland

blocks.html: • Trigeminal nerve (CN V) - most of the facial sensation, and V3 is the motor supply to the chewing muscles

rows: Forehead · upper eyelid · most of the nose
Mid face · lower eyelid · upper lip · beside the orbit
Skin over the mandible · in front of the ear · side of the scalp
Mental nerve · auriculotemporal nerve (runs with the superficial temporal vessels; ear, scalp, temporomandibular joint)
Skin over the angle of the mandible
From the cervical plexus, ventral rami of C2 and C3

blocks.cap: Sensory supply of the face: frontal, infraorbital, mental and auriculotemporal nerves, and the great auricular nerve over the angle of the jaw

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the cranial cavity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Epidural = middle meningeal artery under the pterion, lucid interval, lens-shaped; subdural = torn bridging veins, elderly, slow, crescent. Subarachnoid hemorrhage = ruptured aneurysm, thunderclap headache, stiff neck. Uncal herniation: falling consciousness + same-side blown pupil. Superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1, VI; rotundum V2; ovale V3; spinosum the middle meningeal artery; jugular foramen IX, X, XI. Cavernous sinus: III, IV, V1, V2 in the wall; CN VI and the internal carotid inside. The middle cerebral artery is not part of the circle of Willis.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The skull is a closed box, so anatomy predicts the emergency: which bone breaks over which artery, which foramen carries which nerve, which layer of meninges a bleed sits in, and how cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flows - each tells you what the patient will show.
1. Bones, sutures and weak spots
• Neurocranium: frontal · 2 parietal · occipital · 2 temporal · sphenoid · ethmoid, locked together by immovable sutures

• Fontanelles: soft gaps in the infant skull · allow moulding at birth and brain growth · usually close by 8-12 months · feel them to judge hydration and intracranial pressure
  • Craniosynostosis: sutures close early → the skull grows parallel to the fused suture → abnormal head shape (early sagittal fusion = scaphocephaly) · may raise intracranial pressure, delay development, cause seizures or blindness if not corrected
  • Pterion: where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid meet · the thinnest spot, lying over the middle meningeal artery → fracture here → epidural hematoma
  • Sphenoid: butterfly-shaped, lesser and greater wings · holds the sella turcica (pituitary) and sphenoid sinus · ethmoid: crista galli (attaches the meninges), cribriform plate, perpendicular plate (nasal septum), ethmoid sinuses · petrous temporal: thick, holds the vestibular apparatus
  • Skull fractures: the inner table is thinner and can break with the outer intact · linear (most common) · depressed (bone pushed onto brain) · comminuted (many pieces) · contrecoup (opposite the blow)
2. Cranial fossae and foramina

rows: CN III, IV, V1, VI + ophthalmic veins
CN V3 · accessory meningeal artery · lesser petrosal nerve
CN IX, X, XI · sigmoid sinus → internal jugular vein
Brainstem/spinal cord · vertebral arteries · CN XI (on its way up)

blocks.cap: Anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae seen from above

blocks.html: 3. Arterial supply

• Internal carotid enters through the carotid canal → runs through the cavernous sinus → ends as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
  • Vertebral arteries (from the subclavian) climb through the cervical transverse foramina → foramen magnum → join as the basilar artery → posterior cerebral arteries
  • Circle of Willis = anterior communicating · anterior cerebral · internal carotid · posterior communicating · posterior cerebral - the middle cerebral artery is not part of it · it lets the carotid and vertebral systems back each other up

rows: Medial frontal and parietal lobes · olfactory bulb and tract · corpus callosum
Medial and inferior temporal and occipital lobes

blocks.html: • CN III runs between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries - an aneurysm of either can compress it

blocks.cap: The circle of Willis and the vertebrobasilar system from below

blocks.html: 4. Meninges, spaces and bleeds

• Dura mater: tough, two layers · periosteal (stuck to bone, stops at the foramen magnum, so epidural anesthesia cannot rise into the skull) · meningeal (continues as the spinal dura and folds inward)
    • folds: falx cerebri (between hemispheres) · tentorium cerebelli (cerebrum above, cerebellum below) · falx cerebelli · diaphragma sellae (roof over the pituitary)
    • sensory supply: CN V above the tentorium, C2-C3 below · dural pain is referred as headache
  • Arachnoid: thin, avascular · arachnoid granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses · pia: clings to the brain

rows: Skull and periosteal dura - a potential space (sources differ: the note also says between the two dural layers - check the slides)
Arachnoid and pia - a real space with CSF
Ruptured aneurysm of the circle of Willis
Arterial, fast · brief loss of consciousness → lucid interval → drowsiness, coma
Venous, slow · elderly (brain shrinkage) · may appear weeks to months later · vague: memory loss, confusion
"Worst headache of my life" (thunderclap) · stiff neck · reduced consciousness

blocks.alt: epidural vs subdural hematoma CT - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Axial CT: lens-shaped epidural hematoma and crescent subdural hematoma

blocks.html:
• Herniation: a supratentorial mass (most adult masses; children's are mostly infratentorial) pushes the uncus through the tentorial notch
    • uncal herniation triad: reduced consciousness · same-side fixed dilated pupil (CN III) · irregular breathing → respiratory arrest · if unrelieved, tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum → death
  • Meningitis: headache, fever, drowsiness → sepsis, coma, death · Kernig (straightening the leg hurts) · Brudzinski (lifting the head lifts the legs) · neck stiffness · diagnose by lumbar puncture
5. Venous sinuses

• Lie between the two dural layers and drain to the internal jugular vein
  • Flow: superior sagittal + straight (from inferior sagittal and great cerebral vein) + occipital → confluence → transverse → sigmoid → jugular foramen
  • Cavernous sinus (either side of the sella): CN III, IV, V1, V2 in the wall · internal carotid and CN VI inside
    • face veins connect to it through the ophthalmic veins → infection of the "danger area" (forehead, eyes, nose, lips) can spread in
    • Cavernous sinus syndrome: orbital or facial pain · orbital swelling, chemosis · fever · oculomotor and trigeminal palsies · causes: thrombosis (most common), carotid aneurysm or fistula, meningioma, pituitary tumour
  • Emissary veins have no valves → scalp infection can reach the sinuses
6. Ventricles and CSF

• CSF is made by the choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → interventricular foramen → third ventricle (between the thalami) → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → lateral and median apertures → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → venous sinuses
  • Hydrocephalus is a learning objective but neither source describes it - check the slides

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Cortex
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the cortex
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Broca's aphasia: halting speech, intact comprehension, aware; Wernicke's aphasia: fluent nonsense, poor comprehension, unaware. Motor cortex is precentral, sensory postcentral, and both serve the opposite side. A frontal eye field lesion turns the eyes toward the lesion. Left parietal = Gerstmann syndrome; right parietal = neglect. Bilateral hippocampal damage = anterograde amnesia; mammillary bodies = Wernicke-Korsakoff. Orbitofrontal disinhibition vs medial frontal apathy vs dorsolateral poor planning.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Function is mapped onto the cortex, so a deficit points to a place: learn each area as where it is → what it does → what a lesion looks like, then the white matter that links the areas and the limbic circuit that makes memory.
1. Grey matter, layers and types of cortex

• Grey matter (cell bodies) on the surface · white matter (myelinated tracts) underneath · more grey matter deep in the basal ganglia
  • Six layers: molecular · external granular · external pyramidal · internal granular · internal pyramidal · multiform
    • input arrives in layer 4 (thickest in primary sensory cortex) · layers 3 and 5 send output (thickest in primary motor cortex) (sources differ: the note puts thalamic input in the molecular layer, the upper-year notes in layer 4 - check the slides)
  • Primary areas receive or execute with little interpretation (motor, somatosensory, visual, auditory) · association areas sit next to them and interpret (premotor, somatosensory association) · multimodal association areas combine senses with memory and plan responses (prefrontal)
2. Area by area

rows: Working memory · attention · executive function · problem-solving
Personality change, poor judgement, impulsivity, poor planning
Voluntary movement of the opposite side via the corticospinal tract · laid out as the motor homunculus (the hand gets a large area)
Voluntary, saccadic and pursuit eye movements
Sensation from the opposite side · sensory homunculus
Builds an understanding of the object felt
Passes written words to Wernicke's area · numbers
Left: Gerstmann syndrome - trouble writing, trouble with arithmetic, finger agnosia, right-left confusion · right: neglect of one side of body or space
Receptive aphasia · prosopagnosia (cannot recognize faces) with other temporal damage
Primary visual (by the calcarine sulcus) · visual association
Occipital seizures start with visual hallucinations (flashing or coloured lights)
Balance awareness · taste · sensation from chest and abdominal organs

blocks.cap: Primary motor cortex on the precentral gyrus

blocks.html: • Visual streams: dorsal = "how" (motion, fast, guides action, viewer-centred) · ventral = "what" (detail, slow, recognition, linked to long-term memory)
3. Aphasias
• Testing language: naming · comprehension (one-, two-, three-step motor commands) · fluency (it does not have to make sense to be fluent) · repetition
4. White matter

rows: Regions in the same hemisphere (short: neighbouring gyri · long: different lobes)
Corona radiata → internal capsule → corticospinal tract

blocks.cap: Association, commissural and projection fibres on a coronal section

blocks.html: 5. Limbic system and memory

• Limbic system: emotion, motivation, learning, memory, homeostasis · damage → strange eating and drinking, sexual behaviour change, rage, personality change
  • Hippocampus (deep medial temporal lobe, under the lateral ventricle's inferior horn): forms new memories, turns short-term into long-term · place cells for spatial memory
    • bilateral damage → anterograde amnesia (patient H.M., after bilateral medial temporal resection for epilepsy)
  • Amygdala (in front of the hippocampus): emotion, fear, emotional memory · overactivity → fear, anxiety, aggression (post-traumatic stress disorder)
  • Mammillary bodies (hypothalamus): Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in long-standing alcohol use
    • acute triad: ataxia · eye movement abnormalities · confusion · survivors: anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, poor judgement
  • Cingulate gyrus: above the corpus callosum
  • Papez circuit: cingulate → hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → mammillothalamic tract → thalamus → back to cingulate
    • Alzheimer's disease (early anterograde amnesia) and transient global amnesia both involve it
  • Memory types: sensory (fleeting) → short-term (small, temporary) → long-term (consolidated, usually permanent) · forgetting = decay or overwriting · Alzheimer's disease loses cholinergic neurons

rows: Apathy, low motivation, flat affect, social withdrawal
Perseveration, poor sequencing, rigid thinking, distractible, poor planning and working memory

blocks.cap: The Papez circuit: cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, thalamus

lectures.name: Introduction to Neurophysiology
lectures.title: Introduction to neurophysiology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The action potential is all-or-none: strength is coded by firing frequency, never by size. Myelin gives saltatory conduction; multiple sclerosis strips it and slows conduction. fMRI shows active grey matter (blood flow); DTI shows white matter tracts (water along axons). Glutamate excites and GABA inhibits in the brain; glycine inhibits in the spinal cord. Wernicke's: fluent, cannot understand, unaware; Broca's: effortful, understands, aware.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Symptoms follow from how neurons signal: an all-or-none action potential, sped up by myelin, handed across a synapse as excitation or inhibition. Break a step - strip the myelin, damage a language area - and you can predict what the patient shows. (The note covers only the "need to know" slides 5-8 and 22-23; the synapse section comes from the upper-year notes.)
1. Imaging how the brain works

• The brain is 1-3% of body mass but uses about 20% of its energy, so only a few neurons fire at once
  • Grey matter needs more oxygen than white matter, and blood is sent to the grey matter in use
    • functional MRI (fMRI) detects that change in blood flow → shows which cortex is active in a task
  • Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI): water diffuses along axons in white matter rather than in all directions → shows white matter tracts
  • Dense interconnection lets a focus of abnormal activity spread → why the cortex is prone to epilepsy
2. The neuron

rows: Junction of soma and axon - where the action potential starts
Carries action potentials over long distances
Contact with the next neuron · site of many drugs and toxins

blocks.cap: A neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, myelinated axon with nodes of Ranvier, axon terminal

blocks.html: 3. Membrane potential and the action potential

• Resting potential about −65 mV - the inside is negative
    • depolarization = less negative (toward 0) · hyperpolarization = more negative
  • A depolarizing stimulus that reaches threshold (about −55 mV) at the axon hillock fires an action potential
    • all-or-none: every action potential is the same size - no half action potentials
    • it travels the whole axon by activating each segment in turn
  • Signal strength is coded by frequency, not size
    • how hard = firing rate and how many axons fire · how long = duration of firing · where = which axons fire · what = which receptors (labelled lines: the brain reads any signal on the optic nerve as vision)
  • Myelin insulates the axon → the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) → much faster
    • demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis) makes conduction slow and unreliable

blocks.cap: Ion movements at rest, during depolarization, repolarization and the return to rest

blocks.html: 4. The synapse

• The action potential reaches the terminal → calcium-triggered release of neurotransmitter → binds receptors on the next cell → cleared by diffusion, reuptake or enzyme breakdown
  • Convergence (many neurons onto one: comparing, extracting features) · divergence (one onto many: coordinating movement)

rows: Excitatory (depolarizing): glutamate in the brain · acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction · inhibitory (hyperpolarizing): GABA in the brain (target of many sedatives) · glycine in the spinal cord

blocks.html:
• Excitatory and inhibitory inputs add up over space and time; if the sum reaches threshold, the next neuron fires
  • Transmitter classes: amino acids (GABA, glutamate, glycine) · amines (acetylcholine, dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin) · peptides (substance P, dynorphin)
  • Drugs act as agonists, antagonists, or block reuptake or breakdown · e.g. the GABA-A receptor has several binding sites - benzodiazepines act more strongly with alcohol
  • Learning: the NMDA glutamate receptor opens only on an already-depolarized cell → synapses that fire together strengthen ("cells that fire together wire together")
5. Aphasia: when the language circuit breaks

rows: Fluent, normal rate and syntax, but nonsense words
Slow and effortful, though answers are appropriate

lectures.name: Orbital Anatomy
lectures.title: Orbital anatomy
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ "LR6, SO4, the rest 3": a third nerve palsy leaves the eye down and out with ptosis, a fourth nerve palsy up and in, and a sixth nerve palsy cannot look outward. The floor breaks in a blowout fracture (teardrop sign). Ciliary body makes aqueous humor, Schlemm's canal drains it - blocked drainage is glaucoma. Pupil constrictor = parasympathetic (III); dilator = sympathetic. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy suggests compression. Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden blindness, cherry-red spot.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Every orbital symptom points to a structure: know which walls break, where the eye's fluid is made and drained, and which nerve moves each muscle - then a blowout, a high-pressure eye, a droopy lid or a wandering eye tells you what is damaged.
1. The bony orbit

blocks.lead: A cone of bone that holds the eye, which sits mostly in fat.
rows: Frontal bone (+ lesser wing of the sphenoid)
Zygomatic bone + greater wing of the sphenoid
Maxilla (+ small parts of zygomatic and palatine)

blocks.html: (sources differ: the note puts the ethmoid at the back of the orbit and the lacrimal bone at the back-and-middle; the upper-year notes put both in the medial wall - check the slides)

• Blowout fracture: a blow to the eye pushes out the weak floor or medial wall
    • floor fracture: orbital fat herniates into the maxillary sinus → "teardrop sign" on imaging

rows: Optic nerve (cranial nerve II) + ophthalmic artery
Superior orbital fissure (between the two sphenoid wings)
Cranial nerves III, IV, VI · branches of the ophthalmic nerve (V1: lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary) · superior and inferior ophthalmic veins
Infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) + infraorbital artery

blocks.cap: The seven bones of the orbit with the optic canal and the superior and inferior orbital fissures

blocks.html: 2. The eyeball: layers and chambers

• Outer (fibrous) layer
    • Sclera = tough white coat, where the extraocular muscles insert · cornea = its clear front, where light enters
  • Middle (vascular) layer
    • Choroid = vessels + pigment that stops light scattering
    • Ciliary body = muscle that changes lens shape + processes that make aqueous humor
    • Iris = coloured ring around the pupil (see section 3)
  • Inner layer: retina = rods and cones
    • Optic disc = where the optic nerve leaves: no photoreceptors → blind spot
    • Macula with the fovea in its centre = sharpest vision
  • Chambers
    • anterior (cornea to iris) and posterior (iris to lens) chambers: watery aqueous humor
    • vitreous chamber: gel-like vitreous humor that holds the retina in place
  • Aqueous flow: ciliary body → posterior chamber → through the pupil → anterior chamber → drained at the angle into Schlemm's canal → veins
    • drainage blocked → ↑ pressure inside the eye = glaucoma → presses on the retina → blindness if untreated
  • Lens: hung from the ciliary body by suspensory ligaments
    • ciliary muscle contracts → ligaments slacken → lens rounds up for near vision · lost with age (presbyopia, by about 45)
    • clouded lens = cataracts (damaged, misfolded lens proteins, e.g. from sunlight)

blocks.cap: Layers of the eyeball: sclera, choroid and retina; cornea, iris, ciliary body, lens and conjunctiva

blocks.html: 3. Iris and pupil

rows: Parasympathetic: cranial nerve III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves
Sympathetic: superior cervical ganglion → long ciliary nerves

blocks.html: 4. Eyelid, conjunctiva and tears

• Conjunctiva: palpebral part lines the lid, bulbar part covers the eye (not the cornea) → together a conjunctival sac · secretes lubricating mucus
    • infection = conjunctivitis (pink eye)
  • Lacrimal gland (upper outer orbit) makes tears
    • parasympathetic supply from the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) - via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, reaching the gland in the lacrimal branch of V1
  • Tear drainage: blinking sweeps tears from lateral to medial → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → nasal cavity (inferior meatus)
    • infected lacrimal sac = dacryocystitis
  • Tarsal glands (in the lid): oil that keeps tears on the cornea · clogged or infected = stye (warm compresses; minor surgery if needed)
  • Levator palpebrae superioris lifts the lid: skeletal fibres (cranial nerve III, voluntary) + smooth fibres (sympathetic, widen the eyes in danger)
    • so ptosis (droopy lid) comes from either a third nerve palsy or Horner's syndrome
5. Extraocular muscles

rows: IV (trochlear) - runs through a pulley, the trochlea
Up and out - the only one that does not start at the back of the orbit (starts on the medial floor)

blocks.html:
• The superior and inferior recti also pull the eye inward because the orbit points outward at an angle to the line of sight
  • "LR6, SO4, the rest 3"

blocks.alt: extraocular muscles anterior view - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The extraocular muscles seen from the front: the four recti and two obliques around the eyeball

blocks.html: 6. Nerves and palsies

• Optic nerve (II) = vision · runs through the optic canal in a sheath of meninges with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
  • III, IV, VI enter through the superior orbital fissure · ophthalmic nerve (V1) = sensation from the orbit, upper lid and conjunctiva
  • At rest the muscles balance each other, so a palsy lets the unopposed muscles pull the eye → double vision (diplopia)

rows: Down and out (lateral rectus + superior oblique unopposed)
Ptosis · may have a large pupil - pupil fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so compression (e.g. aneurysm) takes the pupil; a pupil-sparing palsy suggests ischemia (e.g. diabetes)
Head tilt · often trauma or congenital - the least worrying
Turns the head toward the bad side to stop double vision · can be the first sign of ↑ intracranial pressure (long course from the brainstem)
Small pupil, mild ptosis, no sweating - sympathetic supply lost

blocks.html: 7. Blood supply

• Ophthalmic artery = first branch of the internal carotid inside the skull · enters through the optic canal
    • central retinal artery runs inside the optic nerve to the retina → occlusion = sudden, complete blindness · pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula
  • Veins: superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus · inferior ophthalmic vein → pterygoid plexus

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Vision
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of vision
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm: a chiasm lesion gives bitemporal hemianopia; anything behind the chiasm gives a homonymous hemianopia on the opposite side. Near vision = ciliary muscle contracts, lens rounds. Fovea = cones only, sharpest vision; periphery = rods, dim light. Glaucoma takes the periphery first, macular degeneration the centre, cataract blurs everything. Light reflex: in via II, out via III, both pupils constrict.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The lens focuses light, the retina turns it into signals, and the pathway sorts those signals by visual field on the way to the occipital cortex - so the shape of a field defect tells you where the lesion is.
1. Focusing the image: accommodation
• The lens bends light to land a sharp, upside-down image on the retina; it changes shape to keep the target in focus (accommodation)

• Ageing: the lens stiffens and stays too flat → near objects blur → reading glasses (presbyopia)
  • Eyeball shape off: can't see far (myopia) → concave lens · can't see near (hyperopia) → convex lens

blocks.cap: Accommodation: a rounder lens focuses a near target, a flatter lens a far one

blocks.html: 2. Pupillary light reflex

• Bright light → pupil constricts → protects the photoreceptors from saturating and sharpens the image
  • Light in one eye constricts both pupils (consensual) - if not, something is wrong with the nerves or brainstem
  • In: optic nerve (cranial nerve II) → Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain → out: parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) → ciliary ganglion → constrictor muscle
  • A subcortical reflex - tests II, III and the midbrain, not the visual cortex

blocks.alt: pupillary light reflex pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The pupillary light reflex: retina and optic nerve to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, back out via nerve III and the ciliary ganglion to both pupils

blocks.html: 3. The retina

• Light passes through every layer to reach the photoreceptors at the back
  • Five cell types: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells (the only ones that fire action potentials; their ~1 million axons form the optic nerve) · horizontal and amacrine cells link neighbours sideways
  • Phototransduction: light closes sodium channels → the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes → releases less transmitter · darkness does the opposite

rows: Low - many converge on one ganglion cell (large receptive field)

blocks.html:
• Optic disc = blind spot: no photoreceptors where the axons leave · lies nasal to the fovea, so the blind spot is in the temporal visual field · the brain fills it in
  • Reading in dim light is hard: you rely on rods, which are not in the fovea
  • Ganglion cells: P cells (~90%, small fields, colour and fine detail, fed by cones) and M cells (large fields, motion and flicker, fed by rods) · their centre-surround fields pick out edges
  • Colour blindness: ~8% of males (X-linked), ~0.5% of females · red-green is the usual form
4. Diseases of the eye

rows: ↑ pressure in the eye squeezes ganglion-cell axons
Fatty deposits or abnormal new vessels under the macula distort the retina

blocks.html: 5. Central visual pathway and lesions

• The image is reversed: the right visual field lands on the left half of each retina
  • Optic nerve (one eye, both halves of its field) → optic chiasm: fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross (they see the temporal field) → optic tract carries the opposite visual hemifield from both eyes
    • (sources differ: the note says fibres from the "nasal visual field" cross; the upper-year notes say the nasal retina - which sees the temporal field - and the note's own worked example agrees with that - check the slides)
  • ~90% → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (V1) around the calcarine sulcus, occipital lobe
  • ~10% → midbrain: superior colliculus (orienting) · Edinger-Westphal nucleus (pupillary light reflex)

rows: Homonymous hemianopia - the same half in both eyes, opposite the lesion

blocks.alt: visual hemifields to optic nerves chiasm and tracts - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Each visual hemifield reaches both eyes; after the chiasm, the left field travels in the right optic tract and the right field in the left

blocks.html: • Beyond V1: a dorsal "where/action" stream to the parietal lobe (damage → can't guide reaching by sight, optic ataxia) and a ventral "what" stream to the temporal lobe (damage → can't recognise objects, visual agnosia, or faces, prosopagnosia)

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the brainstem, basal ganglia and diencephalon
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Direct pathway (D1) releases the thalamus = GO; indirect pathway (D2, through the external pallidus and subthalamic nucleus) inhibits it = NO-GO - lose nigral dopamine and you get Parkinson disease (too little GO); lose the striatum and you get Huntington chorea (too little NO-GO). Thalamus relays every sense but smell. Hypothalamus = visceral and endocrine control. Corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. The cerebellum works on the same side of the body.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The structures at the core of the brain, and what each one does: the diencephalon relays and regulates, the basal ganglia pick which movement goes ahead, the brainstem carries the tracts and cranial nerve nuclei, and the cerebellum coordinates.
1. Diencephalon

blocks.lead: The grey-matter core of the forebrain, wrapped by the cerebral hemispheres.
rows: Centre of the brain · ~80% of the diencephalon
The relay: every sense except smell has a thalamic nucleus that sends to its primary cortex · organizes, amplifies or dampens signals · held under constant inhibition by the basal ganglia
Between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies · pituitary hangs below
Visceral control centre: autonomic system, temperature, hunger and thirst, sleep-wake, endocrine control, memory, behaviour, emotion
Secretes melatonin in low light (light input relayed from the suprachiasmatic nucleus) → circadian rhythm, sleep
Subthalamic nucleus - part of the basal ganglia circuit

blocks.html:
• Thalamic nuclei
    • relay: ventral posterior lateral (VPL) = body sensation · lateral geniculate = vision · medial geniculate = hearing
    • motor: ventral anterior (input from the globus pallidus) · ventral lateral (input from the cerebellum)
    • limbic and association: anterior (limbic) · medial dorsal (from the amygdala) · pulvinar (to the parietal cortex)
  • Hypothalamic zones: periventricular (hormone output - paraventricular and arcuate nuclei) · medial (limbic links) · lateral (dopamine and serotonin fibres passing through - the reward pathway)

blocks.cap: The thalamic nuclei: sensory relay, motor, limbic and higher-order groups

blocks.html: 2. Basal ganglia: the parts
Deep grey-matter nuclei that release the wanted movement and suppress the rest (also roles in cognition, learning and emotion).

• Striatum = the input: caudate nucleus (arches over the thalamus, beside the lateral ventricle) + putamen · the nucleus accumbens is the ventral striatum
  • Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus
    • external globus pallidus (GPe) = the indirect pathway's relay · internal globus pallidus (GPi) = the output to the thalamus
  • Subthalamic nucleus - excites the internal globus pallidus in the indirect pathway
  • Substantia nigra (midbrain) - its dopamine neurons modulate the striatum · another part suppresses the superior colliculus to stop unwanted eye movements
  • Loop: cortex → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus → motor cortex
3. Direct vs indirect pathway

blocks.lead: At rest the internal globus pallidus fires steadily and keeps the thalamus inhibited.
rows: Cortex → striatum ⊣ internal pallidus ⊣ thalamus → motor cortex
Cortex → striatum ⊣ external pallidus ⊣ subthalamic nucleus → internal pallidus ⊣ thalamus
Parkinson disease: nigral dopamine neurons lost → too little GO → bradykinesia
Huntington disease: caudate and putamen degenerate → too little NO-GO → chorea

blocks.html: (→ excites · ⊣ inhibits)

blocks.cap: Direct pathway: striatum inhibits the internal globus pallidus, releasing the thalamus to drive the motor cortex
Indirect pathway: through the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, ending in more inhibition of the thalamus

blocks.html: 4. Brainstem

blocks.lead: Midbrain, pons and medulla: carries the tracts between brain and cord, holds the cranial nerve nuclei (III to XII), and runs heart rate, breathing, sleep and eating.
rows: Cerebral aqueduct ringed by periaqueductal grey (pain suppression) · red nucleus · substantia nigra
Bulge of pontine nuclei, with the corticospinal tract running through
Pontine nuclei relay the cortex to the opposite cerebellum (middle peduncle)
Pyramids (corticospinal) → pyramidal decussation at the bottom · olives (to the cerebellum)
Autonomic and breathing control near the midline

blocks.html:
• Fourth ventricle lies over the upper medulla and lower pons · the cord's central canal opens into it at the obex
  • Reticular formation: arousal, pain modulation, autonomic reflexes, movement · central pattern generators
  • Tracts passing through: up - spinothalamic, dorsal column-medial lemniscus, spinocerebellar · down - corticospinal, corticobulbar
  • Cranial nerve nuclei: sensory-only nerves (I, II, VIII) and motor-only nerves (III, IV, VI, XI, XII) have one nucleus each · mixed nerves (V, VII, IX, X) have several
  • Where III to XII leave: midbrain III-IV · pons V-VIII · medulla IX-XII (see 04 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy)
5. Cerebellum

• Posterior fossa, under the tentorium · grows out of the pons · cortex of folia, white matter, deep nuclei
  • Controls the same (ipsilateral) side of the body - unlike the motor cortex
  • Compares the planned movement with body position and ongoing movement, then corrects the cortex · motor memory
  • Somatotopy: vermis (midline) = trunk · paravermis = limbs
  • Peduncles: superior → midbrain · middle → pons · inferior → medulla

rows: Balance, vestibulo-ocular reflex, trunk and limb stability
Anterior lobe (note) · vermis + intermediate zone (upper-year notes)
Adjusts ongoing trunk and limb movement and tone

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the spinal tracts and cerebellum
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Dorsal columns cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross in the cord where they enter, and the lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramids - so a one-sided cord lesion takes vibration, position and power on its own side but pain and temperature on the other. Spinocerebellar tracts end up on the same side. Gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm. UMN facial weakness spares the forehead. Sensory = 3 neurons through the VPL; motor = 2 neurons, UMN and LMN.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.
Every tract question comes down to two facts: what it carries, and where it crosses. Put those together and a lesion's level and side tell you which modalities go, and on which side.
1. How the pathways are built

• Ascending (sensory) tracts usually have 3 neurons; descending (motor) tracts have 2 - an upper motor neuron and a lower motor neuron
  • Named origin → destination (spinothalamic = spinal cord → thalamus) · paired left and right · most cross the midline (decussate)
  • Sensory chain
    • 1st order: cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar), brings the signal into the cord
    • 2nd order: cell body in the dorsal horn or a brainstem nucleus; its axon crosses and runs to the thalamus
    • 3rd order: ventral posterior lateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • Motor chain
    • upper motor neuron (UMN): cell body in the cortex or brainstem; axon crosses and synapses on a lower motor neuron
    • lower motor neuron (LMN): cell body in the ventral horn (body) or a cranial nerve motor nucleus (head) → muscle

blocks.alt: spinal cord cross-section ascending and descending tracts - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Spinal cord cross-section: ascending tracts (blue) and descending tracts (red), with the sacral-to-cervical layering inside each

blocks.html: 2. The tract table

cols: Sign of a one-sided cord lesion
rows: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus (gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm)
Medulla - 2nd-order axons cross as the medial lemniscus
Lost on the same side below the lesion
Spinal cord, at the level of entry - anterior white commissure
Lost on the opposite side below the lesion
Posterior: never · anterior: crosses twice - both end on the same side
UMN weakness on the same side below the lesion
~10% stay uncrossed until their level, then act on both sides
Muscles of the head and face via cranial nerve nuclei
Mostly both sides - except the lower face (VII), opposite side only

blocks.html: 3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus

• 1st order: up the same side in the fasciculus gracilis (leg) or fasciculus cuneatus (arm)
  • 2nd order: nucleus gracilis / nucleus cuneatus in the medulla → axons cross → medial lemniscus → VPL
  • 3rd order: VPL → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • (sources differ: one section of the note says the nucleus gracilis takes sensation from above T6 (arms) and the cuneatus from below; the note's own pathway section and the upper-year notes say gracilis = leg (below T6), cuneatus = arm - check the slides)

blocks.alt: medulla oblongata cross-section (nucleus gracilis, nucleus cuneatus, and medial lamniscus).png
blocks.cap: The medulla: nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send fibres across the midline to form the medial lemniscus

blocks.html: 4. Spinothalamic tract

• 1st order: synapses straight away in the dorsal horn
  • 2nd order: crosses at once in the anterior white commissure → up the opposite side → VPL
  • 3rd order: VPL → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • Pain and temperature fibres sit toward the edge of the cord
5. Spinocerebellar tracts

• Simplest pathway: no thalamus and no net crossing - unconscious position sense for staying upright
  • 1st order from muscle proprioceptors (spindles, Golgi tendon organs) → dorsal horn
  • Posterior tract: same side → inferior cerebellar peduncle (medulla) · anterior tract: crosses, then crosses back → superior cerebellar peduncle
6. Descending motor tracts

• Lateral corticospinal: primary motor cortex → corona radiata → internal capsule → cerebral peduncle (midbrain) → ventral pons → medullary pyramids → ~90% cross → lateral white column → synapse on LMNs in the ventral horn → limbs
  • Corticobulbar: motor cortex → internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → branches to the pons and medulla → LMNs in the nuclei of III, IV, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII
    • the lower face gets only crossed input, the forehead both → a UMN facial nerve palsy spares the forehead

blocks.cap: Corticobulbar pathway: motor cortex to the cranial nerve nuclei in the pons and medulla

blocks.html: 7. Cerebellar connections

• In: spinocerebellar tracts (inferior and superior peduncles) · corticopontocerebellar: motor cortex → pontine nuclei → cross → middle cerebellar peduncle → cerebellar hemisphere
  • Out: deep cerebellar nuclei → superior peduncle → opposite thalamus (ventral lateral nucleus) → motor cortex
  • Input and output both cross, so the cerebellum acts on the same side of the body

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Sensation
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of sensation
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Vibration, fine touch and position cross in the medulla; pain and temperature cross in the cord where they enter - so a cord hemisection loses position sense on the lesion's side and pain on the other. Pacinian = vibration, Meissner = texture, Merkel = edges, Ruffini = stretch. Test pain or temperature, not touch, to find a segmental level. Burning and freezing are felt by pain receptors. Gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Each skin receptor reports one kind of touch, and two pathways carry it to the cortex - one crossing in the medulla, one in the cord. That split is what lets a cord lesion separate vibration from pain.
1. Receptors in the skin

• Free nerve endings: around hair follicles (very sensitive), pain and temperature
  • Nociceptors (pain)
    • on a myelinated axon: fast, sharp, well localized → can trigger withdrawal
    • on an unmyelinated axon: slow, dull, throbbing, poorly localized
  • Thermoreceptors: one for warm, one for cool · burning or freezing activates pain receptors, not thermoreceptors

blocks.cap: Skin receptors by depth: Merkel disc and Meissner corpuscle near the surface, Pacinian corpuscle and Ruffini ending deep in the dermis

blocks.html: 2. How a stimulus is coded

• Pacinian corpuscle: pressure deforms the capsule → stretch-gated ion channels open → receptor potential → action potential if threshold is reached
  • Stronger, longer stimulus → faster, longer train of action potentials, but the curve flattens at high pressure → easier to tell 4 g from 5 g than 14 g from 15 g
  • Labelled lines: each receptor has its own "private line", so what you feel depends on which axon fires - hitting the ulnar nerve at the elbow (funny bone) is felt in the fingers
  • Acuity: few afferents converge per neuron at the fingertip (small fields, fine two-point discrimination) vs many on the back · centre-surround inhibition sharpens edges
  • Touch is needed for fine motor control: numb the fingertips and lighting a match becomes hard
3. The two pathways

rows: Up the same side in the dorsal column → nucleus gracilis (leg) or nucleus cuneatus (arm) in the medulla
Synapses in the dorsal horn at the level it enters

blocks.html: • Dorsal columns are layered: at the neck, leg fibres lie medially, then trunk, then arm laterally (new fibres join on the outside)

blocks.alt: dorsal column-medial lemniscus vs spinothalamic pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (crossing in the medulla) beside the spinothalamic tract (crossing in the spinal cord)

blocks.html: 4. Clinical use

• Cord hemisection: the tracts run in different columns and cross at different levels, so a right hemisection loses
    • vibration, fine touch and proprioception on the right (same side)
    • pain and temperature on the left (opposite side)
  • Dermatomes (skin supplied by one spinal nerve) overlap - more for touch than for pain and temperature
    • so test pain or temperature to find the level of a segmental nerve injury
5. Somatosensory cortex

• Primary somatosensory cortex = postcentral gyrus · four strips, each with its own body map (homunculus): proprioception · touch · texture · size and shape
  • The map is plastic: a heavily used part grows (a violinist's fingering hand); after an amputation neighbouring areas take over - stroking the face can be felt in the missing hand

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of the Cerebellum and Basal Ganglia
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of the cerebellum and basal ganglia
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cerebellar disease = intention tremor, low tone, signs on the same side, stable or improving; Parkinson disease = tremor at rest, rigidity, trouble starting, progressive - and neither causes weakness. Dopamine turns GO up and NO-GO down: too little → Parkinson, too much levodopa → dyskinesia. Huntington chorea = lost striatum, too little NO-GO. Cerebellar lesions last because the repair shop itself is broken.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Two side loops tune movement without commanding it: the cerebellum corrects errors and learns skills, the basal ganglia choose which movement is released. Damage gives movement disorders without weakness - and the tremor, tone and course tell them apart.
1. Side loops in the motor system

• Both take input from wide areas of the cortex and send output through the thalamus back to the cortex (and to the brainstem)
  • Neither sends its own tract to the spinal cord, so they have no upper motor neurons → not upper motor neuron (UMN) disorders
2. Cerebellum: what it does

• Folded into folia and fissures · holds half of all the brain's neurons
  • Corrects errors in movement commands and learns motor skills
    • in: motor and somatosensory cortex, brainstem, spinal cord · out: motor cortex, brainstem and cord
  • Lesions show on the same side: each half works with the opposite motor cortex, which moves the opposite body - so a right cerebellar lesion affects the right limbs
  • How it learns (upper-year notes)
    • mossy fibres → parallel fibres → Purkinje cell = "what I did" (the student)
    • climbing fibres from the inferior olive = "something is wrong" (the teacher, an error signal) → reshape the parallel-fibre synapses
    • e.g. re-tuning the vestibulo-ocular reflex with new glasses · cerebellar patients cannot adapt their aim when prism goggles shift what they see
  • "Repair shop": it masks motor damage elsewhere, so cerebellar lesions themselves cause longer-lasting problems
3. Cerebellar signs

rows: Wide-based, drunk-looking gait · nystagmus (broken vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Gait ataxia - falls walking heel-to-toe · hypotonia
Dysmetria (misses the target) · dyssynergia (body segments poorly coordinated) · intention tremor (worst at the end of a movement) · fails finger-to-nose

blocks.html: • Romberg (feet together, eyes open then closed): sways with eyes open and closed = cerebellar · sways only with eyes closed = sensory ataxia (sources differ: the upper-year notes also list a Romberg sign under vestibulocerebellar damage - check the slides)

blocks.alt: cerebellum functional zones vermis intermediate lateral - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Cerebellum from behind: vermis, intermediate and lateral zones; anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes
Finger-to-nose: a normal straight path against the wandering path of cerebellar dysmetria

blocks.html: 4. Basal ganglia: release and suppress

• Release the wanted movement, suppress the inappropriate ones from the premotor and motor cortex · damage contributes to Tourette syndrome (inappropriate utterances released)
  • In: cortex → striatum (caudate + putamen) · out: globus pallidus → thalamus → cortex
  • Modulators: subthalamic nucleus → globus pallidus · substantia nigra → striatum
  • Dopamine from the substantia nigra excites the direct pathway (GO) and damps the indirect pathway (NO-GO)
  • Eye movements: the substantia nigra holds the superior colliculus in check; the striatum lifts that brake to release a saccade
5. Basal ganglia disorders

• Levodopa = dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier - the main treatment for Parkinson disease
  • (sources differ on Huntington: the note says ↑ dopamine causes the under-inhibition; the anatomy lecture note and the upper-year notes blame loss of the striatum's indirect pathway - check the slides)
6. Cerebellar disease vs Parkinson disease

rows: Ataxia: starts, but inaccurate (dysmetria) and poorly coordinated (dyssynergia)
Akinesia: can't start (may need an outside cue) · bradykinesia: slow
Intention - end of a movement, none at rest

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Reflexes
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of reflexes
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Upper motor neuron lesion = spastic, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing big toe, no wasting (flaccid only in the first days); lower motor neuron lesion = flaccid, absent reflexes, fasciculations, wasting. Spindle = length, Ia, monosynaptic stretch reflex; Golgi tendon organ = force, Ib, relaxes the muscle. Small, fatigue-resistant units are recruited first. Fasciculation = whole motor unit (visible); fibrillation = one fibre (EMG only). Supplementary motor area lesion → apraxia.
